text: A glossary with ten terms works fine as a flat, alphabetical list. A glossary with three hundred terms doesn't — without structure, someone searching for Revenue has no way to discover that Net Revenue and Gross Revenue are closely related terms they might actually need.
Flat lists make browsing nearly impossible, which defeats a large part of what a glossary is for. Glossaries typically model three relationship types to fix this.

Hierarchy — broader and narrower, Revenue is broader than Net Revenue. Synonym — two terms meaning exactly the same thing, with one marked as official and the other pointing to it. And related term — connected, but not a hierarchy and not a true synonym.

Here's a worked hierarchy. Revenue branches into Gross Revenue, Net Revenue, and Recognized Revenue — and Net Revenue branches further into North America and International. Each child term still needs its own specific, measurable, self-contained definition, not just 'Net Revenue, but regional' left implicit.

Watch for the synonym trap: Customer and Account often get treated as the same thing colloquially, but a customer might have multiple accounts. Marking them as true synonyms would silently lose a distinction the business relies on — related term is the honest relationship there. Next lesson: building a business glossary — putting all four lessons together into one real artifact.
